title: Luqman's advice to his son
hook: Luqman the wise tells his son: don't associate anything with Allah (31:13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, aya, and your line was difference is a sign. Did you try the greeting, and how did it land? Day five hundred thirty-three, and a new surah.

Some advice from a parent arrives at a big moment: leaving home, a wedding, a hospital bed. Some arrives over the washing up, and only years later turns out to have stuck. Surah Luqman, the thirty-first, is named for a man the Qur'an calls wise, and at its heart is a father talking to his son, piece by piece. The Qur'an keeps his words, and lets us listen in. Today, the first line.

Who was Luqman? The Qur'an says only that God gave him wisdom, hikma, and that the first thing wisdom meant was: give thanks to God. Beyond that, the sources are quiet. Later tradition says he was from Africa, perhaps Nubia or Abyssinia, and reports differ on whether he was a tailor, a carpenter or a shepherd. Scholars have asked whether he was a prophet; tradition mostly remembers him as a wise man. The Qur'an doesn't settle it. What it does give is his words. Pickthall: "O my dear son! Ascribe no partners unto Allah. Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong." Start with the first three words. In Arabic, ya bunayya. Not just my son, ibni, but the small, tender form, bunayya: my little son, my dear boy. The weightiest advice in the speech starts with affection. Then the content. Ascribing partners is shirk: treating anything else, money, power, a person, an idol, as if it shared God's place. And he calls it zulm 'azim, a tremendous wrong, an injustice. The classical dictionaries define zulm as putting something where it doesn't belong. There's a hadith in Bukhari that shows how much this verse mattered. When another verse said that safety belongs to those who don't mix their faith with zulm, the companions were frightened: which of us hasn't wronged himself? And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told them it doesn't mean that; it means what Luqman told his son, that shirk is a tremendous wrong. So the first advice is about putting first things first. Before manners, before prayer, before how to walk and talk, which come later in the speech: know who God is, and don't put anything in His place.
screen: `WHO WAS LUQMAN? THE QUR'AN IS QUIET.` · `YA BUNAYYA: MY DEAR SON.` · `SHIRK: A TREMENDOUS WRONG.` · `FIRST THINGS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pass on one piece of good advice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the best advice anyone ever gave you, the one that actually changed something. Who gave it? How did they say it? Was there tenderness in it? Now think of someone younger, or newer, who might need it: a child, a niece, a new colleague, a friend going through what you went through. Picture how you'd say it, starting the way Luqman did, with affection. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Luqman. The wise man of surah thirty-one, whose speech to his son starts, my dear son, and puts first: don't ascribe partners to God. Today's word.
Your line: the first advice. Today, give the advice you thought of to the person you pictured, and begin it kindly. Day five hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Muslim parents and teachers often use Luqman's advice in 31:13–19 as a model for raising children, beginning with tawhid, the oneness of God.

what it means: a father's speech that starts with tenderness and puts God first, before every other piece of advice.
what a scholar hears: ya bunayya, the diminutive; shirk as zulm 'azim; and Bukhari's report linking 6:82 to 31:13.
